etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English craft (“strength, skill”), from Old English cræft (“strength, skill”), from Proto-West Germanic *kraftu, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz (“strength, power”); further origin obscure. Cognate with German Kraft (“strength, power, force, energy, employee”) and Danish kraft (“strength, power, force”).

definitions.definition: (uncountable, obsolete) Strength; power; might; force [9th century].

quote.citation: 1526, William Bonde, Pylgrimage of Perfection‎[1]:
quote.text: By the craft of nature.

definitions.definition: Ability, skilfulness, especially skill in making plans and carrying them into execution; dexterity in managing affairs, adroitness, practical cunning; ingenuity in constructing, dexterity [9th century].

quote.citation: 1846, George Grote, A history of Greece:
quote.text: The Cyclôpes were Brontês, Steropês, and Argês,—formidable persons, equally distinguished for strength and for manual craft  […]

quote.citation: 2016 June 11, Phil McNulty, “England 1-1 Russia”, in BBC Sport‎[2]:
quote.text: England should have had enough against a very ordinary Russia to complete the job but Rooney's removal robbed them of his craft and guidance and now increases the pressure on Thursday's meeting with Wales in Lens.

definitions.definition: Cunning, art, skill, or dexterity applied to bad purposes; artifice; guile; subtlety; shrewdness as demonstrated by being skilled in deception [13th century].

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Mark 14:1:
quote.text: […] and the chiefe Priests, and the Scribes sought how they might take him by craft, and put him to death.

quote.citation: 1651, Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, or The Matter, Forme, & Power of a Common-wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill, London:  […]  [William Wilson] for Andrew Crooke, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  you have that Crooked Wisdome, which is called Craft  […]

quote.citation: 1904, Jack London, The Sea-Wolf (Macmillan’s Standard Library), New York, N.Y.: Grosset & Dunlap, →OCLC:
quote.text: We have not the strength with which to fight this man; we must dissimulate, and win, if win we can, by craft.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Occult art, magic [13th century].
(uncountable) Intellectual power; skill; art.
(collective or plural) Handmade items, especially domestic or decorative objects; handicrafts [20th century].

quote.citation: 1911 January, Timberman:
quote.text: [Canton] has a large export trade in hand-made crafts, ivory and furniture.

definitions.definition: (countable, obsolete in the general sense) A work or product of art [c. 1000].
(countable, obsolete) A device, a means; a magical device, spell or enchantment [13th century].

quote.citation: c. 1440, Generydes. A royal historie of the excellent knight Generides:
quote.text: For your entente I shall a craft devise […] That ye shall haue your purpose euery dele.

definitions.definition: (countable, obsolete) Learning of the schools, scholarship; a branch of learning or knowledge, a science, especially one of the ‘seven liberal arts’ of the medieval universities [13th century].

quote.citation: a. 1325, Cursor Mundi, page 272:
quote.text: […] Þe seuen craftes all he can […]

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Skill, skilfulness, art, especially the skill needed for a particular profession [9th century].

quote.citation: 1640, Ben Jonson, Timber: or Discoveries made upon Men and Matter, page 213:
quote.text: A poem […] is the work of the poet; the end and fruit of his labour and study. Poesy is his skill or craft of making; the very fiction itself, the reason or form of the work.

quote.citation: 1678, Joseph Moxon, Mechanick exercises, or The doctrine of handy-works:
quote.text: It is counted […] good workmanship in a Joyner, to have the craft of bearing his hand so curiously even, the whole length of a long Board.

definitions.definition: (countable, plural crafts) A branch of skilled work or trade, especially one requiring manual dexterity or artistic skill, but sometimes applied equally to any business, calling or profession; the skilled practice of a practical occupation [since the 9th century].

quote.citation: 1847, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Evangeline, A Tale of Acadie, page 281:
quote.text: […] For since the birth of time, throughout all ages and nations, / Has the craft of the smith been held in repute by the people.

quote.citation: 1871, Edward Augustus Freeman, The history of the Norman conquest, page 250:
quote.text: Fond as William was of the craft of the woods, he was the least likely of all men to let his sport stand in the way of his interest.

quote.citation: 1991, James Munson, The Nonconformists: In Search of a Lost Culture, "The+great+preachers+were+masters+of+their+craft"&dq="The+great+preachers+were+masters+of+their+craft"&hl=de&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwiXrqf9pNjcAhXEa1AKHQ3RBD8Q6AEIJzAA page 113:
quote.text: The great preachers were masters of their craft.

quote.citation: 2021 September 8, Phil McNulty, “Poland 1-1 England”, in BBC Sport‎[3]:
quote.text: This was billed as the battle between Kane and his Poland opposite number Lewandowski but this was a game where it was possible to simply enjoy two masters of their craft at work.

definitions.definition: (countable) A trade or profession as embodied in its practitioners collectively; the members of a trade or handicraft as a body; an association of these; a trade's union, guild, or ‘company’ [15th century].
(nautical) Boats, especially of smaller size than ships. Historically primarily applied to vessels engaged in loading or unloading of other vessels, as lighters, hoys, and barges.

quote.citation: 1951 October, R. S. McNaught, “Lines of Approach”, in Railway Magazine, page 705:
quote.text: Quite near could also be seen several ancient wooden warships, and always a variety of craft slipping up and down the tideway.

definitions.definition: (nautical, British Royal Navy) Those vessels attendant on a fleet, such as cutters, schooners, and gun-boats, generally commanded by lieutenants.
(figurative) A woman.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter IX, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “A tight little craft,” was Austin’s invariable comment on the matron; and she looked it, always trim and trig and smooth of surface like a converted yacht cleared for action.

definitions.definition: (countable, plural craft) A vehicle designed for navigation in or on water or air or through outer space [since the 17th century].
(countable, fishing) Implements used in catching fish, such as net, line, or hook. Modern use primarily in whaling, as in harpoons, hand-lances, etc. [17th century].

quote.citation: a. 1784, T. Green, “An Act for encouraging and regulating Fiſheries”, in Acts and Laws of the State of Connecticut, in America, page 79:
quote.text: And whereas the continual Interruption of the Courſe and Paſſage of the Fiſh up the Rivers, by the daily drawing of Seins and other Fiſh-Craft, tends to prevent their Increaſe, […]

quote.citation: 1869 April 27, C. M. Scammon, “On the Cetaceans of the Western Coast of North America”, in Edward D. Cope, editor, Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia, volume 21, page 46:
quote.text: The whaling craft consists of harpoons, lances, lines, and sealskin buoys, all of their own workmanship.

quote.citation: a. 1923, Charles Boardman Hawes, “A Boy Who Went Whaling”, in The Highest Hit: and Other Selections by Newbery Authors, Gareth Stevens Publishing, published 2001, →ISBN, page 47:
quote.text: From the mate’s boat they removed, at his direction, all whaling gear and craft except the oars and a single lance.

quote.citation: 1950, Discovery Reports, volume 26, Cambridge University Press, page 318:
quote.text: […] Temple, a negro of New Bedford, who made ‘whalecraft’, that is, was a blacksmith engaged in working from iron the special utensils or ‘craft’ of the whaling trade.

quote.citation: 1991, Joan Druett, Petticoat Whalers: Whaling Wives at Sea, 1820–1920, University Press of New England, published 2001, →ISBN, page 55:
quote.text: The men raced about decks collecting the whaling craft and gear and putting them into the boats, while all the time the lookouts hollered from above.

definitions.definition: To make by hand and with much skill.
To construct, develop something (like a skilled craftsman).
(video games) To combine multiple items to form a new item, such as armour or medicine.
